Senses.Explanation: Stop, stop, no need to speak; my way is wondrous, beyond thinking — the Lotus assembly's own refusal, taken over by the Chan hall as its standing seal for what words cannot carry, then beaten, blinded, and re-spoken from a whisk-tip for eight hundred years. The oldest retained use is an answer, not a lecture. In Zhaozhou Congshen's record a monk asks: the one who comes thus — do you receive him? Receive. The one who come not-thus — do you receive him too? Receive. Then: the thus-comer you receive from the master; the not-thus-comer — how do you receive him? Stop, stop — no need to speak; my way is wondrous, beyond thinking. The question about how is sealed with the refusal itself: what receives is not a how. Dachuan Puji, closing a cascade of exchange-questions in the Tianning hall — the lotus-peak hut-master's three self-answers fielded one by one (tell it to no sorrowful man; say it to a sorrowful man and you kill him; staff across the shoulder, straight into a thousand peaks — cheeks behind the skull, have no dealings) — then says: stop, stop — no need to speak, my way is wondrous, beyond thinking. Spitting blood at a man defiles first one's own mouth. The bell not yet struck, the drum not yet sounded — Tianning has already eaten his thirty blows. Know where this lands, and you too may rightly eat thirty. And Zhanran Yuancheng, raising the Lotus lecture for the officials: of the four lines I opened with, one kills and quickens; the old man of the Sakyas strained his utmost and got only half. Why? Stop, stop — no need to speak; my way is wondrous, beyond thinking. Light is not shining on a world, the world is not there to hold; light and world both forgotten — what is it then? His whisk between his brows casts the white-tufted beam to eighteen thousand lands: lift your eyes and it blinds them; lean your ear and it stops them; raise a thought and it shatters the heart — eye cannot see it, ear cannot hear it, mind cannot think it. At just such a time the old monk passes you word: a golden oriole up the tree, one branch of gold; a white egret down the field, a thousand points of snow. Tianyin Yuanxiu, answering for the speechless: a monk died, went into the dark, and met the Earth-store bodhisattva, who asked — what did you work at all your life? I recited the Lotus. Then this line — stop, stop, no need to speak, my way is wondrous, beyond thinking — is it speaking, or is it not speaking? The monk had no word. Tianyin answers in his place: thank you for the instruction. Yinyuan Longqi, holding up the whisk: the old man of the Sakyas has come — on the tip of this mountain monk's whisk he says stop, stop — no need to speak; my way is wondrous, beyond thinking. Trust it and each of you sits steady at home, nothing left undone; fail, and this monk will weave brambles to tangle your feet. One stroke of the whisk through the air: one-two-three-four-five, out springs a pack of tigers; five-four-three-two-one, the returning phoenix has no peer; one-five-two-four-three, dragons and elephants interweave; three-one-five-two-four, each shows its handle. The spirit-workings of all buddhas and patriarchs have leaked out entire — say, on whose grace-strength does such marvel rest? Long silent: in youth he broke the dragon-snake battle-line; grown old and stooped, he still hearkens to the little boys' song. And Qingzhong Tiebi Huiji in the hall: the tortoise crawling to the fire — the machine unbroken before the eon; the pestle blooming — the intent handed down outside the teaching. Bare and far-standing, hills bright, waters fair; solitary and gleaming, suns go, moons come. The cypress-nut before the court shows its machine even now; the peach-blossom behind the seat already mirrors its color. Just at such a time — whose family's tune is it? The staff cracks: stop, stop — no need to speak; my way is wondrous, beyond thinking.
